approaches.name: Combined dorsal and palmar approach to perilunate injuries
approaches.corridor: Radially based dorsal capsular flap combined selectively with an extended carpal-tunnel exposure to the palmar carpus

sources.title: Combined approach to perilunate fractures and dislocations
A comparison of outcomes in acute perilunate injuries

procedure_applications.condition: Dorsal reduction alone is inadequate or palmar lunate displacement, median-nerve compression, osteochondral injury, or volar soft-tissue interposition requires direct access

positioning.text: Position supine with the arm on a radiolucent hand table, forearm freely rotatable, and the hand accessible from both dorsal and palmar sides.

setup.text: Prepare the forearm and hand circumferentially, obtain provisional reduction when safe, document median-nerve status, and confirm complete PA and lateral fluoroscopic access.

surface_landmarks.text: Dorsally mark Lister tubercle, radial and ulnar styloids, DRUJ, and third CMC joint; palmarly mark palmaris longus, wrist creases, fourth ray, and carpal-tunnel course.

incision.text: Start with an approximately 8-cm longitudinal dorsal incision from proximal-ulnar to Lister tubercle toward the third CMC joint; add an extended carpal-tunnel incision only when palmar access is required.

superficial_interval.text: Dorsally protect radial sensory branches, release EPL from the third compartment, retract second-compartment tendons radially, and elevate the fourth compartment ulnarly; palmarly elevate flaps ulnar to palmaris longus and open the carpal tunnel under direct protection.

deep_interval.text: Raise a radially based dorsal capsuloligamentous flap while preserving its radial attachment and the radiolunotriquetral insertion; through the palmar window, protect the median nerve and retract flexors to inspect volar ligaments and interposed tissue.

layers.text: Dorsal skin, retinaculum and extensor compartments, dorsal capsule, then carpus; palmar skin, palmar aponeurosis and antebrachial fascia, flexor retinaculum, median nerve and flexors, then palmar capsule and ligaments.

structures_encountered.text: EPL, second and fourth extensor compartments, posterior interosseous nerve, dorsal capsular ligaments, proximal carpal row, median nerve, flexor tendons, ulnar neurovascular bundle, and palmar carpal ligaments define the exposure.

structures_at_risk.text: The median nerve and recurrent motor branch, radial sensory branches, EPL and extensor tendons, dorsal radioulnar ligament, TFCC, intrinsic carpal ligaments, and articular cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Divide the flexor retinaculum ulnar to the median nerve over a blunt protector, preserve the radial capsular insertion, and do not injure the dorsal radioulnar ligament or TFCC near the DRUJ.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid fixed pressure on the median nerve and avoid tensioning superficial sensory branches or extensor tendons; release exposure longitudinally rather than retracting harder.

exposure.text: The dorsal window surveys the proximal row, intrinsic ligaments, and midcarpal joint; the palmar window decompresses the carpal tunnel and permits removal of palmar interposition and repair of volar injury.

limitations.text: Dual exposure increases soft-tissue dissection and is not required when stable anatomic reduction and all necessary repairs can be achieved dorsally; comparative evidence has not shown one approach universally superior.

extensions.text: Extend the dorsal incision proximally or distally as needed; add the palmar limb for irreducible volar displacement, median-nerve decompression, or palmar tissue interposition rather than using it routinely.

indications.text: Use combined exposure for selected irreducible perilunate or lunate dislocations, trans-scaphoid patterns with volar interposition, osteochondral injury, or combined dorsal and palmar ligament pathology requiring direct repair.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid the additional palmar exposure when dorsal reduction is anatomic and stable, median-nerve decompression is unnecessary, and no volar pathology requires treatment.

implant_implications.text: Plan intercarpal wires, screws, and ligament anchors so they restore carpal alignment without tethering extensor tendons or penetrating radiocarpal and midcarpal cartilage.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm scapholunate and lunotriquetral relationships, capitate-lunate alignment, carpal height, fracture reduction, and safe implant position on PA, lateral, and oblique views.

closure.text: Repair the dorsal capsular flap, close the third compartment without EPL constriction or leave EPL superficial if glide is limited, and close the palmar wound without reconstituting carpal-tunnel compression.

complications.text: Complications include recurrent instability or reduction loss, median or sensory-nerve injury, tendon adhesion or rupture, stiffness, diminished grip, infection, osteonecrosis, and post-traumatic arthritis.

bailouts.text: If the lunate or carpus remains irreducible dorsally, stop forceful manipulation and add the palmar exposure to remove interposed tissue under direct vision.

questions.question: Which approach is generally performed first for a perilunate injury?
What are key reasons to add the palmar exposure?
questions.answer: Irreducible palmar lunate or carpal displacement, palmar soft-tissue interposition, osteochondral pathology, or median-nerve decompression.

questions.question: On which side of the median nerve is the flexor retinaculum divided?
questions.answer: On its ulnar side, over a blunt protector.

approaches.name: Dorsal approach to the finger carpometacarpal joints
approaches.corridor: Longitudinal dorsal interval between extensor tendons centered over the injured CMC joint or joint cluster

sources.title: Dorsal approach to the carpometacarpal joints
Fracture dislocations of the carpometacarpal joints of the fingers
Management of fracture-dislocations of the little finger carpometacarpal joint
Dorsal approach to CMC joint (middle-phalanges collection)
Dorsal approach to CMC joints (metacarpals collection)

procedure_applications.condition: A second-through-fifth CMC dislocation or fracture-dislocation is irreducible, unstable, chronic, or blocked by interposed tissue

positioning.text: Position supine with the hand pronated on a radiolucent table and fingers free for rotational assessment and fluoroscopy.

setup.text: Prepare the full hand and wrist, assess all adjacent CMC joints, and ensure PA, lateral, and oblique imaging because overlapping anatomy can conceal malalignment.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark affected metacarpal shafts and bases, neighboring CMC joints, extensor tendon paths, and planned wire exit zones.

incision.text: Use a longitudinal incision from the metacarpal base toward the proximal carpal row between extensor tendons, centered over the affected joint or between multiple involved joints.

superficial_interval.text: Protect dorsal sensory branches and longitudinal veins, identify intertendinous connections, and mobilize extensor tendons with their loose surrounding tissue radially or ulnarly.

deep_interval.text: Use the traumatic capsular rent in acute injuries or perform a limited formal capsulotomy in partially healed or chronic cases to remove blocks and restore the CMC articulation.

layers.text: Skin, dorsal sensory branches and veins, extensor tendon interval with juncturae, dorsal capsule, then metacarpal base and distal carpal row.

structures_encountered.text: Dorsal veins, radial and ulnar sensory branches, extensor tendons and juncturae, dorsal CMC capsule, metacarpal bases, and distal carpal row are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Dorsal sensory nerves, extensor tendons and intertendinous connections, CMC cartilage, and nearby deep motor or vascular structures are at risk from dissection and fixation.

danger_zones.text: Retract radial sensory branches radially and ulnar sensory branches ulnarly; enlarge exposure rather than stretching a nerve across the operative field.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid focal traction on sensory branches and preserve tendon gliding by retracting tendons with their surrounding tissue and minimizing central wire-tendon conflict.

exposure.text: Provides direct visualization of one or several dorsal CMC joints to remove interposed tissue, reduce articular fragments, and stabilize the metacarpal bases.

limitations.text: A single narrow interval may not safely expose widely separated radial and ulnar injuries, and volar pathology or neurovascular compression may require a separate approach.

extensions.text: Lengthen proximally and distally or use separate tendon-respecting windows for multiple joints rather than excessive transverse undermining.

indications.text: Use for irreducible, unstable, delayed, or multiply injured finger CMC dislocations and fracture-dislocations requiring direct reduction or fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Open exposure is unnecessary when early closed reduction is anatomic, stable, and maintainable without tendon or nerve compromise.

implant_implications.text: Place K-wires or screws to stabilize the injured ray to a stable adjacent metacarpal or carpus while avoiding central extensor-tendon tethering and articular penetration.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use true lateral plus PA and oblique views to confirm parallel CMC joint lines, restoration of metacarpal cascade, articular reduction, and safe hardware.

closure.text: Repair the capsule with nonabsorbable suture, repair any divided intertendinous connection, verify tendon glide, and close skin without nerve entrapment.

complications.text: Complications include missed residual dislocation, reduction loss, sensory neurapraxia or neuroma, extensor adhesion, stiffness, pin infection, post-traumatic arthritis, and weakness.

bailouts.text: If one incision cannot safely expose multiple joints, use an additional tendon-respecting window; if reduction remains blocked, directly identify the interposed capsule, tendon, or fracture fragment.

questions.question: What determines incision placement for multiple CMC injuries?
questions.answer: It is centered between the affected joints while respecting extensor tendons.

questions.question: Which superficial structures require protection?
questions.answer: Dorsal sensory nerve branches and longitudinal veins.

questions.question: What must be repaired if divided during exposure?
questions.answer: The dorsal capsule and any cut intertendinous connection.

approaches.name: Ulnar approach to the hook of hamate
approaches.corridor: Ulnar palmar exposure through Guyon-canal territory with direct identification and mobilization of the ulnar nerve and artery to the hamate hook

sources.title: Ulnar approach to the hamate hook
Surgical management of hook of hamate fractures: a systematic review
Excision of hook of hamate fractures in elite baseball players

procedure_applications.condition: A symptomatic hook fracture or nonunion requires excision or fixation, or selected pisiform pathology requires excision

positioning.text: Position supine with the forearm supinated on a hand table and the wrist gently extended and radially deviated to expose the ulnar palm.

setup.text: Prepare the hand and distal forearm, confirm the target on CT or appropriate imaging, and have microsurgical instruments available for ulnar neurovascular dissection.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark FCU, pisiform, palpable ulnar artery radial to FCU, hamate hook distal-radial to the pisiform, DRUJ level, and distal palmar crease.

incision.text: Use an approximately 5-cm zigzag incision beginning radial to FCU at DRUJ level, turning near the pisiform and distal palmar crease, then continuing distally in the hypothenar palm.

superficial_interval.text: Open antebrachial fascia proximally, identify the ulnar artery and nerve before entering Guyon canal, and divide palmaris brevis distally under direct vision.

deep_interval.text: Trace and protect the ulnar neurovascular bundle distally, retract it ulnarly, divide hypothenar origins from the hook as needed, and expose the hook subperiosteally.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, antebrachial fascia and palmaris brevis, Guyon canal with ulnar nerve and artery, hypothenar origins and pisohamate ligament, then hamate hook periosteum.

structures_encountered.text: FCU, pisiform, ulnar artery and nerve, superficial and deep ulnar branches, palmaris brevis, pisohamate ligament, flexor retinaculum, hypothenar origins, flexor tendons, and hamate hook are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: The ulnar artery, superficial sensory and deep motor branches of the ulnar nerve, superficial palmar arch, flexor tendons, and motor branches to hypothenar muscles are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The deep motor branch curves around the hook and the superficial palmar arch lies nearby; identify neurovascular anatomy before circumferential hook dissection or fragment removal.

retraction_hazards.text: Use gentle intermittent ulnar retraction of the nerve and artery and avoid traction transmitted to the deep motor branch around the hook.

exposure.text: Provides direct circumferential access to the hook for fragment excision or fixation and can be extended to selected pisiform excision or ulnar-tunnel decompression.

limitations.text: The approach places the ulnar neurovascular bundle directly in the operative field; excision changes ligament and hypothenar attachments and is not automatically preferable to fixation in every patient.

extensions.text: Extend proximally for Guyon-canal decompression or toward the pisiform for post-traumatic pisiform excision while maintaining direct control of ulnar nerve branches.

indications.text: Use for symptomatic displaced hook fractures, painful hook nonunion, fragment excision in selected athletes, ORIF in selected reconstructable fractures, and selected post-traumatic pisiform sequelae.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid fragment excision when preservation of hook biomechanics is prioritized and stable fixation is feasible; reassess the plan when ulnar neurovascular scarring makes safe mobilization uncertain.

implant_implications.text: For ORIF, choose a trajectory that captures the hook without entering adjacent joints or impinging the ulnar nerve or flexor tendons; after excision, remove all sharp residual prominence.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use dedicated carpal-tunnel or tangential views to localize the hook, verify complete excision or reduction, and confirm safe fixation when screws are used.

closure.text: Confirm intact ulnar-nerve branches and flexor glide, repair divided hypothenar fascia as appropriate without recreating compression, and close the zigzag skin incision without tension.

complications.text: Complications include transient or permanent ulnar sensory or motor dysfunction, vascular injury, scar pain, residual fragment pain, flexor-tendon irritation, weakness, infection, and reoperation.

bailouts.text: If scar or variant anatomy prevents safe hook access, extend Guyon-canal exposure and identify both superficial and deep ulnar branches before proceeding; do not remove the fragment blindly.

questions.question: What forms the borders of Guyon canal at the hamate level?
questions.answer: The pisiform medially and hook of hamate laterally; the canal contains the ulnar nerve and artery.

questions.question: Which ulnar-nerve branch is especially vulnerable around the hook?
Which muscles originate from the hook and may require release?
questions.answer: Flexor digiti minimi brevis and opponens digiti minimi.
